title: Architectural Thinking
subtitle: See the forces behind a design decision
summary: Pip sketches the growing bookshop, then a developer finds a boundary that makes testing awkward. Architectural thinking connects structure with implementation feedback, broad alternatives, and business priorities. Pip stays hands-on without becoming the person every release must wait for.

concepts.title: Architecture and design
concepts.body: Pip’s proposed bookshop service boundary makes a core workflow difficult to test. Architecture addresses structure, characteristics, patterns, and major components; design supplies detailed classes, screens, and code. The porous boundary needs feedback in both directions. Pip joins the developers, revises the seam, and records the rationale while change is still inexpensive.

concepts.title: Breadth and depth
concepts.body: Pip almost chooses last year’s database without considering alternatives. Architectural breadth means recognizing technologies, patterns, and constraints well enough to ask useful questions. A few deep areas sustain practical judgment without demanding mastery of everything. Pip compares relational storage, event streams, and caches, then prototypes the plausible fits.

concepts.title: Trade-off analysis
concepts.body: Pip’s rare-book auction needs both analytics and controlled payment access. Publish-subscribe eases new consumers and producer decoupling; queues isolate contracts, access, and consumer scale. Budget, skills, culture, time, environment, and priorities change the balance. Pip records benefits, liabilities, the local choice, and the assumption that would justify revisiting it.

concepts.title: Business drivers
concepts.body: Pip hears “finish pricing by closing time” and asks what happens after an interruption. Growth may imply scale and elasticity; critical workflows may need reliability, recovery, and auditability. Words such as fast or available hide different thresholds. Pip works with domain stakeholders to turn business meaning into prioritized structural concerns.

concepts.title: Hands-on without bottlenecks
concepts.body: Pip volunteers to own the framework every release depends on, then notices the bottleneck. Hands-on architecture can instead use production-quality prototypes, debt work, fixes, automation, fitness functions, and reviews. Pip compares caching approaches and automates a dependency check while developers own delivery. Real implementation evidence improves later decisions without centralizing critical-path work.

misconceptions.claim: Architecture is a document handed from an architect to developers, after which design begins.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter presents architecture and design as synchronized, iterative work. A one-way handoff loses implementation feedback and lets architectural drift go unnoticed.

misconceptions.claim: The most extensible or technically sophisticated option is automatically the best architecture.
misconceptions.correction: Extensibility is only one benefit. Security, contract flexibility, observability, scaling, cost, and team context can make a less extensible option the least-worst choice.

scenario.title: Route bids to three consumers
scenario.context: An auction platform captures bids and sends them to tracking, analytics, and history. History needs a richer contract than the other consumers, while security and independent consumer scaling matter during bidding bursts. The team expects more consumers later, but the current platform can monitor queues more precisely than a shared topic. Choose a communication shape and explain which risk the business is willing to carry.

options.label: Publish to a topic
options.benefit: One producer connection makes future consumers easy to add and reduces producer knowledge of consumers.
options.cost: Consumers share a contract and bid data may be visible to more subscribers; per-consumer backlog scaling is less direct.
options.consequence: Bid History subscribes without changing Bid Producer. The team must enforce subscriber authorization and either accept a common schema or add an adaptation layer for richer history data.

options.label: Send through queues
options.benefit: Each consumer can have its own contract, access boundary, backlog, and scaling policy.
options.cost: The producer knows every destination and must change when a new consumer appears, increasing coupling and operational wiring.
options.consequence: History gets its current-price field without disturbing other consumers, and operators can scale analytics separately. Adding a fourth consumer requires producer and infrastructure changes.

scenario.debrief: Neither mechanism wins in the abstract. The topic favors extensibility and producer decoupling; queues favor isolation, heterogeneous contracts, and per-consumer operations. Business priorities and platform capabilities determine the balance.

quiz.question: A developer finds that a proposed architecture makes a workflow difficult to test. What is the strongest architectural response?
options: Treat the architecture as fixed and ask the developer to follow it
Collaborate, revisit the boundary, and evolve the design with implementation evidence
Move all detailed decisions to a separate architecture committee
quiz.explanation: Architecture and design evolve together. Collaboration surfaces a structural problem early; a fixed handoff or distant committee preserves the very barrier that causes drift.

quiz.question: Why might an architect choose a queue instead of a topic for an auction consumer?
options: Queues always have lower latency than topics
Queues allow each consumer to use a separate contract and independently monitored backlog
Queues eliminate every form of coupling between producer and consumer
quiz.explanation: The source identifies consumer-specific contracts, access, monitoring, and programmatic scaling as queue benefits. Queues still couple the producer to destinations, and no mechanism is always faster.

quiz.question: Which activity keeps an architect hands-on while reducing the risk of blocking delivery?
options: Owning the shared framework on the critical path
Writing a production-quality proof of concept or an architecture fitness check
Avoiding source code and relying on diagrams
quiz.explanation: A bounded proof of concept or automated check exercises implementation judgment without making the architect the sole owner of code every developer needs to proceed.

exercise.title: Make a least-worst decision
exercise.prompt: Choose a real or invented system decision. Name the business driver, compare two plausible designs, and record the trade-off you would revisit if the context changed.
